explanations.answer: No one can stand against us
explanations.explanation: That's the point, friend. Paul asks, "If God is for us, who can be against us?" (Romans 8:31). It's a question with no one left standing to answer it. Picture a crowd of opponents all looking at each other and suddenly finding something to do in the other room.

Close, but Paul doesn't promise that. In a few verses he lists trouble, distress and persecution (Romans 8:35), so he knows hard things come. His point is about who is on our side. If God is for us, who can be against us? (Romans 8:31).

explanations.answer: We must earn His help first
explanations.explanation: Nothing in Paul's question asks us to earn anything. He just says, "If God is for us…" and he doesn't add a single condition after it (Romans 8:31). I spent years in a drawer thinking I had to earn my way out. Turns out I had it backwards. God is for us, and that settles who is against us.

Yes, baker! Paul says God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, so "how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things?" (Romans 8:32). Notice the word freely. There's no invoice stuck to the back of this one. If He gave the biggest gift, the rest is no stretch.

explanations.answer: Ask us to pay Him back
explanations.explanation: Nope, and I love that it's nope. Paul says God will "freely give us all things" (Romans 8:32). Freely means no payment plan and no bill showing up later. I've seen a lot of price stickers in my day, and this gift doesn't have one.

explanations.answer: Hold back the rest for now
explanations.explanation: That's not where Paul goes. He reasons that God gave up His own Son for us all, so how will He not also, along with Him, freely give us all things? (Romans 8:32). It's the opposite of holding back. The biggest gift is already given, so the rest follows with it.

That's it, baker. Paul says, "It is God who justifies" (Romans 8:33). The One with the final say is the One who declares us right with Him. So anyone lining up to bring a charge is talking to the wrong office.

Good word, but it's not the one Paul uses. He writes, "Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies" (Romans 8:33). Justifies is the answer to a charge. A warning is a different thing, and it can't answer a charge against someone.

Waiting is something I know plenty about, friend. But Paul doesn't say it here. He says, "It is God who justifies" (Romans 8:33). God isn't sitting on the sidelines while a charge hangs in the air. He's the one who has already settled it.

Not quite, and this one is easy to trip on. Paul asks, "Who is there to condemn us?" and then points to Christ Jesus, who died, was raised to life, and is at the right hand of God (Romans 8:34). So Jesus is not the one condemning. He's the reason there's no one left to.

Right, baker. Paul asks, "Who is there to condemn us?" and then points to Christ Jesus (Romans 8:34). He points to Jesus as the one who died, was raised and is at God's right hand. He is interceding for us, not condemning us. Whew, what a difference one answer makes.

Yes, friend. Trouble, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger and sword are all things people go through (Romans 8:35). Paul names the rough stuff on purpose. None of it is on the list of things that can cut us off from the love of Christ.

I see why you'd think so, but look at the list again. Trouble, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, sword (Romans 8:35). Those are things that happen to people, not things people do. I think Paul wants us to see that even the hardest things we face don't get the last word.

Not this time, baker. Nothing on that list is a rule to follow. Famine, nakedness, danger and sword are things that come at a person (Romans 8:35). It's a list of hard things people suffer, and Paul asks if any of it can separate us from the love of Christ.

That's the opposite of what Paul says. After the list he answers, "No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us" (Romans 8:37). He starts that line with a big, firm No. Trouble, famine and sword are real, but they don't cut us off from the love of Christ.

Right, baker. Paul asks who shall separate us from the love of Christ, lists the hard things, and then says, "No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us" (Romans 8:37). That No is doing a lot of work. Hard things are real, but they can't pull us away from Him.

That's the phrase, friend. Paul says, "No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us" (Romans 8:37). Notice it's through Him who loved us, not through our own muscle. I'd lift my mustache in a victory wave if I could lift it any higher.

I get it, some days feel exactly like that. But Paul says the opposite: "we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us" (Romans 8:37). Even in famine and danger, he doesn't describe hanging by a thread. It's more than conquerors, and it comes through Him who loved us.

Good guess, but Paul says we are in these things, not kept out of them. His words are, "in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us" (Romans 8:37). The hard things are real and we walk through them. The win happens right in the middle, through Him who loved us.

That's it, baker. Paul says, "neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God" (Romans 8:39). Anything else in all creation is a big net. He leaves no corner of it open for something to sneak through.

Rome is where Paul's readers lived (Romans 1:7), so I see why it came to mind. But he goes far past one city. He says, "nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God" (Romans 8:39). Creation covers a whole lot more than one address.

Israel is a fair guess, but Paul's list is bigger than any one nation. He writes, "nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God" (Romans 8:39). Creation is the word he lands on. That's everything, so nothing is left out.

True, friend. Paul ends with "the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:39). After all that building up, he lands on a person, not an idea. That love is found in Christ Jesus, and nothing in all creation can pull us away from it.

Not this time. Paul's last words are that nothing "will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:39). So the love is found in Christ Jesus. It's the very end of the passage, and the line is the point of the whole thing.
